# Unified vs Separated Model Patterns

Trade-offs of SQLModel's "one model for DB + API" versus the traditional
"separate Pydantic + SQLAlchemy" approach.

## The Unified Pattern (SQLModel)

A single class definition serves as both database schema and API model [2][17]:

```python
class Hero(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: int | None = Field(default=None, primary_key=True)
    name: str
    secret_name: str
    age: int | None = None
```

### Advantages

| Advantage | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| DRY | Single definition eliminates field duplication | [2][17] |
| API/DB sync | Changes propagate automatically across layers | [17] |
| FastAPI integration | Seamless request/response validation | [2][18] |
| Conciseness | More readable code from unified definition | [17] |
| Drop-down escape hatch | Can use raw SQLAlchemy when needed | [17][18] |

### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Data exposure risk | Same model for DB and API can expose sensitive data | [3] |
| Performance overhead | 19x slower than plain SQLAlchemy for GROUP BY on millions of rows | [13] |
| Limited ORM flexibility | Abstracts away advanced SQLAlchemy features | [17] |
| Hidden behavior | "Automatic mapping can be magical" | [17] |
| Library coupling | Changes to Pydantic or SQLAlchemy require refactoring | [17] |
| No table validation | table=True silently skips Pydantic validation | [8][9] |

## The Separated Pattern

Distinct Pydantic models for API contracts and independent SQLAlchemy models
for persistence [17][18]:

### Advantages

| Advantage | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Full SQLAlchemy power | Unrestricted access to advanced features | [17][18] |
| Clear architecture | Distinct separation of representation and persistence | [17] |
| Independent evolution | Each layer optimizes separately | [17] |
| Maturity | Both libraries have extensive documentation and community | [17] |

### Disadvantages

| Disadvantage | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Boilerplate | Similar fields defined twice | [17] |
| Sync burden | Manual conversion between Pydantic and SQLAlchemy objects | [17] |
| Consistency risk | API and DB schemas can drift | [17] |

## The Hybrid Reality

Even SQLModel's own documentation acknowledges the unified pattern is
insufficient for real applications [3]:

> "In most cases, there are slight differences" requiring multiple model
> patterns.

The official recommendation is to create a base data model with shared fields,
then inherit into purpose-specific classes [3]:

- `HeroBase(SQLModel)` — shared fields (name, age)
- `Hero(HeroBase, table=True)` — database model with `id`
- `HeroCreate(HeroBase)` — request schema without `id`
- `HeroPublic(HeroBase)` — response schema with required `id: int`

Key guidance: "Only inherit from data models, don't inherit from table models"
[3]. If inheritance creates excessive complexity, "duplicating fields may be
clearer" [3].

## Decision Framework

| Criterion | Choose SQLModel | Choose Separated |
|---|---|---|
| Project size | Small to medium | Large, complex systems |
| Framework | FastAPI prioritizing DRY | Any framework |
| DB complexity | Standard CRUD operations | Advanced features, complex relationships |
| Team experience | Newer to Python ORMs | Deep SQLAlchemy knowledge |
| Performance needs | Standard web loads | Analytical queries, large datasets |

Some roadmap discussion participants concluded they would avoid SQLModel,
finding "duplication of a small amount of code" more maintainable than the
framework's complexity [11].

## Gaps and Limitations

- Limited published case studies from large-scale production deployments
  using SQLModel
- Performance comparison data is sparse — the 19x figure [13] is one data
  point on one query type
- The hybrid reality (needing multiple models anyway) weakens the DRY
  argument that is SQLModel's primary selling point
